summary: This informational document describes a variant of MIKEY that uses Identity-Based Authenticated Key Exchange and a trusted key management service. Clients authenticate each other and derive a session key. It is not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people trust a notary. With the notary's help they prove who they are and build a shared secret for their call.

questions: how does mikey-ibake avoid key escrow
why are time-bound keys better than certificates
subtitle: Key management for multimedia security using identity-based encryption and a trusted key service.

tldr.problem: Multimedia security systems need to establish session keys between two parties and authenticate each other's identities, but traditional public-key infrastructure requires complex certificate management, and standard identity-based encryption has a key escrow problem where the key management service can decrypt all traffic.
tldr.mechanism: MIKEY-IBAKE combines the MIKEY protocol with Identity-Based Authenticated Key Exchange (IBAKE) and a trusted Key Management Service (KMS). Users obtain time-bound credentials from the KMS infrequently, then use identity-based encryption to mutually authenticate and derive session keys without the KMS's involvement in each exchange. The time-bound nature eliminates the need for revocation.
tldr.outcome: Multimedia applications gain a low-operational-cost key management system where the KMS does not need to be highly available, users do not share secrets with the KMS for each session, and key compromise is limited to the time period associated with that key.

facts.label: Key escrow
facts.value: Not present (session key is derived without KMS)

facts.label: Forward secrecy
facts.value: Perfect (each session has unique ephemeral keys)

today: RFC 6267 is Informational and describes a MIKEY extension intended primarily for 3GPP multimedia security. MIKEY remains widely used in the 3GPP ecosystem for protecting voice and video calls. While MIKEY-IBAKE itself has not become a universal standard, the approach of time-bound identity-based credentials has influenced subsequent security protocol design, particularly in scenarios where operational simplicity and limited KMS availability are important.

sections.title: Key Management at Scale
sections.content:
The Multimedia Internet Keying (MIKEY) protocol defines several mechanisms for distributing session keys in multimedia applications, such as those protected by SRTP (Secure Real-time Transport Protocol). Traditional approaches rely either on pre-shared keys (which do not scale to many parties) or public-key infrastructure (PKI), which requires certificates, certificate authorities, and complex revocation procedures.

MIKEY-IBAKE proposes a different model using Identity-Based Encryption (IBE), where a public key is derived directly from an identity string (such as a person's email address). This eliminates the need for certificates. The approach relies on a Key Management Service (KMS) that the users trust, but crucially, the KMS is involved only infrequently—perhaps once a month—rather than in every session setup. In contrast to traditional PKI, where an attacker who compromises the key authority can decrypt all past and future traffic, MIKEY-IBAKE uses time-bound identities. Credentials automatically expire and are valid only on specific dates, limiting the window of exposure if a key is lost.
sections.plainLanguage: Multimedia calls need security. Instead of watching every call, a trusted party gives out daily identity cards that people use to prove themselves to each other. No certificates, no revocation, no key escrow.

sections.title: Identity-Based Encryption and Time-Bound Keys
sections.content:
Identity-Based Encryption is a public-key encryption system where the public key is computed directly from a user's public identity, such as their phone number or email address. No certificate is needed. The private key is issued by a trusted party (the KMS) and changes depending on a date field in the identity. For example, the identity might be encoded as "alice@example.com || 2025-10-18". The KMS generates the private key for this specific combination.

The critical advantage is automatic expiration. Unlike X.509 certificates, which must be explicitly revoked if compromised, a key bound to a specific date simply stops being valid when the date changes. An operator can use one key per day, one per month, or any interval desired. If a private key is leaked on day 1, only day 1's traffic is at risk; day 2's traffic was encrypted with a different key. There is no revocation mechanism needed, no certificate authority overhead, and no periodic renewal.

The system also avoids the key escrow problem. In standard IBE, the KMS that generates private keys could theoretically decrypt any message encrypted with those keys. MIKEY-IBAKE solves this by having users generate a shared session key using elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman, which the KMS never sees. The KMS is involved only in distributing the long-term credentials needed to perform the handshake; it does not have access to the session keys themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: An identity is your email plus a date. The trusted party hands out keys just for that day. Tomorrow it's a different key. Nobody can escape from key escrow because the actual secrets are made between the two people, not given by the trusted party.

sections.title: The Protocol in Three Phases
sections.content:
The MIKEY-IBAKE protocol has three phases. In phase one, the Initiator and Responder independently contact the KMS (possibly different KMSs) and obtain private keys for their identities, using either pre-shared key or public-key authentication. This exchange happens infrequently—perhaps once a month—and does not need to be fast or highly available. Each user gets private keys for multiple dates, reducing the frequency of KMS interaction.

In phase two, the Initiator sends a message to the Responder containing a random elliptic-curve point encrypted using the Responder's public identity (derived from the Responder's identity string and date). The Responder decrypts this using the private key obtained from the KMS, generates its own random point, encrypts the Initiator's point plus identities using the Initiator's public identity, and sends it back. At this point, both parties can compute the same shared secret (based on elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman), which the KMS has never seen.

In phase three, the Initiator and Responder exchange verification messages to confirm they both derived the same secret and know each other's identities. The session key is then derived from this shared secret and used to protect the actual multimedia traffic via SRTP.
sections.plainLanguage: First, both people get daily cards from the trusted party. Then they swap encrypted numbers to prove they're the right people and make a shared secret. Then they swap verification messages and start the secure call.

sections.title: Message Structure
sections.content:
MIKEY-IBAKE messages are built using MIKEY's standard payloads with extensions for identity-based encryption. The messages include a header (containing version and crypto session IDs), a timestamp, and random data for freshness. For messages with the KMS, they additionally include the user's identity, the KMS's identity, and authentication tags. For peer-to-peer messages, they include both parties' identities and IBAKE payloads containing the encrypted elliptic-curve points.

An optional Encrypted Secret Key (ESK) payload can be included to support scenarios where the recipient is not immediately available—for example, a voicemail system that receives a call but the intended recipient is offline. The ESK allows the recipient, when they become available, to retrieve the encryption key needed to decrypt the caller's messages without requiring a new key exchange with the sender.

All encryption in peer-to-peer messages uses Identity-Based Encryption as specified in related RFCs, while the KMS exchange can use simpler encryption based on pre-shared keys or standard public-key methods. This design allows the system to coexist with traditional MIKEY modes.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages have headers, timestamps, and encrypted numbers. Special payloads can leave encrypted keys in a mailbox for people who aren't home yet.

sections.title: Supporting Complex Communication Scenarios
sections.content:
MIKEY-IBAKE supports more than simple point-to-point calls. Forking occurs when a single user is registered at multiple devices (desk phone, laptop, mobile), and an incoming call is delivered to all of them simultaneously. Because identities are bound to the user (not the device), the protocol handles this transparently—multiple devices can respond, and each establishes a session using the same identity.

Retargeting is when a proxy or server redirects a call to a different destination. The protocol supports both scenarios where the originator knows about the redirect and starts fresh with the new destination's identity, and scenarios where the redirection is transparent to the originator. In both cases, the identity-based approach allows the system to generate session keys for the actual communicating parties.

Deferred delivery (such as voicemail) is where a message is stored for later retrieval. The ESK payload allows the sender to securely deliver an encryption key that the recipient's mailbox can store and give to the actual recipient when they become available. This is particularly valuable in multimedia systems where content might be pre-recorded and stored, then delivered later.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone calls you at multiple phones, all of them can answer the same call. If the call is forwarded, it works. If you're not home, your mailbox can save the secret so you can listen when you arrive.
